title: Glade Park Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Glade Park wells have a 495-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $30,800-$49,100.
h1: What Glade Park Wells Cost and How They Perform
intro_html:
Glade Park wells are commonly deep, and most are completed in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Records within five miles show a 495-foot median well depth, with the middle half between 410 and 590 feet. The typical reported yield is 5.0 gallons per minute.

That gives a buyer a useful starting point, but not a guarantee for a specific parcel. Only a portion of the recorded wells report both construction details and pump yield. Before buying land or pricing a home site, review nearby permits, confirm the intended well use, and have a driller evaluate access and geology.

sections.heading: Glade Park well depth reflects fractured ground
sections.html:
Most Glade Park wells are deeper than a typical shallow alluvial well. 68% are between 300 and 600 feet, while 24% are deeper than 600 feet. Only 6% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and just 1% are under 100 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 960 feet.

The records identify 549 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. In this setting, depth can change substantially from one lot to the next as a driller follows water-bearing fractures and usable formations. For bidding, the 410-to-590-foot middle range is more useful than assuming a shallow strike. A quote should state what happens if the hole must go deeper, along with casing, grout, development, pump setting, and testing.

sections.heading: The usual Glade Park yield is usable but not excessive
sections.html:
Among wells reporting pump yield, the median is 5.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 4.0 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 67%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 29% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute.

A five-gallon-per-minute well can serve ordinary household use when storage and pump controls are designed correctly, but it does not automatically support heavy irrigation or high-demand landscaping. The permit use mix is largely domestic or household use at 96%, with stock use reported on 28% of permits and irrigation on 1%. Ask for a sustained yield test, not just a brief recovery reading.

sections.heading: Glade Park water levels show no clear decade decline
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 310 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 246 to 470 feet. That is the depth to the water level when the well is not being pumped, not the total well depth. A pump must be selected around the actual water level, pumping drawdown, well depth, and storage design.

The decade comparison is nearly unchanged: the median was 310 feet in the 2010s and 311 feet in the 2020s. This limited permit record does not show a meaningful broad decline between those periods. It is still not a guarantee for a new lot. Local fractures, seasonal conditions, nearby pumping, and differences in measurement methods can matter more than the area-wide median.

sections.heading: Permit history points to a few recurring drillers
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records include 556 permitted wells within five miles of Glade Park. Of those, 381 are recorded as constructed, 397 report total depth, and 236 report pump yield. The newest permit year is 2025, so the area continues to see well activity rather than being represented only by older construction.

The busiest names in these records are Rocky Mtn Drilling And Pump Services LLC (Logue, James M.) with 178 records, Rocky Mountain Drlg./Pump Svcs (Wisener, A. L.) with 144, and Colorado Drilling Company (Carns, Don R) with 63. Permit history helps identify local experience, but a buyer should still verify current licensing, insurance, references, access requirements, and the exact scope of a new-well contract.

sections.heading: A Glade Park well at median depth can cost substantially more
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in this area, the drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 495-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $24,800 to $37,100. This is the hole itself, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $30,800 to $49,100. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed bid. A contractor should identify mobilization, road and pad work, casing and grout, drilling through difficult formations, water testing, pump installation, and connection to the home. The 410-to-590-foot middle depth range is important when comparing bids because a quote based on a shallow assumption may not match local conditions.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole exposure, and the building site
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about ten miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 historic mine feature. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped information. These records do not prove contamination at a particular well, but they are a reason to test before closing and to ask about nearby land uses, mine workings, and the intended household water source.

Low yield and a dry hole remain possible in fractured bedrock even where nearby wells perform well. Confirm the permit, allowed use, well location, septic separation, driveway access, and a buildable area before purchasing. A septic designer should evaluate soil and setbacks early. The well, septic system, electrical route, tank location, and house foundation need to work together on the actual parcel, not just on a sketch.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Glade Park?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Glade Park is 495 feet. The middle half runs from 410 to 590 feet, and 24% of recorded wells are deeper than 600 feet. Most are in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, so the depth on a nearby parcel is a useful guide but not a guarantee.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Glade Park?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 495-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $24,800 to $37,100. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $30,800 to $49,100. Site access, difficult formations, and the final pump system can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Glade Park wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 5.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 4.0 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. Have the specific well tested and size storage for the intended household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Glade Park?
faq.a: The mapped area includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 historic mine feature, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those records do not determine water quality at a parcel. Test the well for the contaminants relevant to the site and proposed use, and review the results before relying on the water for a home.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Glade Park?
faq.a: Reported static water levels had a median of 310 feet below surface in the 2010s and 311 feet in the 2020s. That limited comparison does not show a meaningful broad decline. The middle half of reported static levels is 246 to 470 feet, and conditions can vary considerably between fractured-bedrock wells on nearby lots.
